connection: Session 18 introduced interface-based polymorphism for a production repository. TimeClock still has no genuine class hierarchy, so inheritance is practiced in a Session 19 ScratchPad class instead of inventing policies in Domain.
objectives: Distinguish an abstract base class from an interface.
Implement an abstract member with override.
Reuse one protected concrete helper from two related derived formatters.
Judge why this demonstration belongs in ScratchPad rather than TimeClock production code.

visuals.title: Formatter is an incomplete base
visuals.explanation: Formatter requires Format but supplies Normalize. It cannot be constructed directly.

visuals.title: Two related types inherit one helper
visuals.explanation: UpperFormatter and LowerFormatter both are Formatters and reuse Normalize rather than duplicating trimming behavior.

visuals.title: override fulfills the abstract member
visuals.explanation: The compiler checks each Format override against Formatter.Format.

visuals.title: Interface or abstract class?
visuals.explanation: Use an interface for a capability and substitution boundary; use an abstract class only for a genuine related family that benefits from shared implementation.

preQuiz.prompt: Why is this lesson in ScratchPad?
options: TimeClock has no verified class-hierarchy requirement
preQuiz.explanation: Do not invent a hierarchy for the product.

preQuiz.prompt: Can an abstract class be instantiated directly?
preQuiz.explanation: It is an incomplete base for derived types.

preQuiz.prompt: What must a concrete derived class do with an abstract member?
preQuiz.explanation: The override supplies the missing implementation.

concept.title: Abstract classes combine requirements and shared code
paragraphs: An abstract member requires each derived type to provide behavior. A concrete member supplies shared behavior once.
ScratchPad is appropriate because TimeClock's production variation is already modeled naturally with interfaces.

concept.title: Derived types override required behavior
paragraphs: A derived class uses override to fulfill the abstract contract. It inherits concrete members without copying them.
The hierarchy should represent a genuine is-a relationship, not a desire to reuse a few lines.

concept.title: Interfaces and abstract classes solve different problems
paragraphs: Interfaces describe capabilities across otherwise unrelated implementations. Abstract classes model a related family that benefits from shared implementation.
The production repository boundary needs substitution, not a shared base implementation, so it remains interface-based.

lab.objective: Build one small formatter hierarchy to observe abstract, protected, inherited, and overridden members without changing the TimeClock design.
lab.startingCondition: Session 19 has no dedicated ScratchPad class. Production uses IClockEntryRepository and has no verified need for inheritance.
lab.keyPointTitle: Inheritance must represent a real relationship
keyPoints: Formatter cannot be constructed because it is abstract.
Normalize is protected: derived classes can call it, unrelated callers cannot.
This ScratchPad example does not create a production HoursPolicy hierarchy.
steps: Declare a public sealed Session19InheritanceDemo class.
Below the demo class, declare an abstract Formatter class.
Add an abstract string Format(string value) member.
Add a protected static Normalize method that trims the supplied text.
Declare a sealed UpperFormatter class that inherits Formatter.
Override Format and return the normalized text in uppercase.
Declare a sealed LowerFormatter class that inherits Formatter.
Override Format and return the normalized text in lowercase.
In Run, declare a Formatter variable that refers to an UpperFormatter.
Call Format with text containing surrounding spaces and display the result.
Reassign the same variable to a LowerFormatter and display the second result.
Try to construct Formatter directly, observe the compiler error, then comment out that line.
Add a Session 19 call in ScratchPad/Program.cs without deleting earlier session calls.

steps.text: Run ScratchPad and build the solution, then compare with the collapsed solution.
steps.code:
dotnet run --project src/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.ScratchPad/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.ScratchPad.csproj --configuration Release
dotnet build PinkMachine19.TimeClock.sln --configuration Release && dotnet test PinkMachine19.TimeClock.sln --configuration Release --no-build

reveals.title: Solution
reveals.text: Use this only after your own attempt.

lab.expectedBehavior: ScratchPad prints TIME CLOCK and time clock. Production remains unchanged.

postQuiz.prompt: When is an abstract class a good fit?
options: For a related family with shared implementation
postQuiz.explanation: Both relationship and shared behavior should be meaningful.

options: They need substitutable capabilities, not inherited implementation
postQuiz.explanation: The design pressure is substitution across storage implementations.

postQuiz.prompt: What happens to the concrete helper on a derived class?

reflections: Why is Formatter a more honest inheritance example than inventing HoursPolicy classes in Domain?
What does Normalize share that an interface contract alone would not store?
What evidence would make inheritance appropriate in production?
whatBreaks: Constructing Formatter directly fails because it is abstract. Omitting either Format override leaves a concrete derived class incomplete. Making Normalize private prevents derived formatters from using it; making it public exposes a helper callers do not need.
summary: Session 19 uses a contained formatter hierarchy to show abstract requirements, protected shared implementation, and override. TimeClock production remains interface-based because no real class hierarchy has been established.
